title: Plate Tectonics and Mountain Formation
seo_title: Grade 10 Science: Plate Tectonics and Mountain Formation Worksheets (MATATAG)
short_title: plate boundaries, volcanoes and mountain building
standard_code: Grade 10, Quarter 1: Earth and Space Science
standard_text: Plate movement at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries forms mountains, trenches, volcanoes and earthquakes; mantle convection drives the plates. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 10, Quarter 1: Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Earth and Space Science): tsunamis and volcanoes, plate tectonics, plate boundaries and crust age, mantle convection and plate motion and plates in motion. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Most volcanoes are at plate boundaries.
key_sub: Silica-rich magma is sticky and explosive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plates move apart at divergent boundaries, collide at convergent boundaries and slide past at transform boundaries. Subduction zones make deep trenches, volcanic arcs and large earthquakes; continental collisions build mountain ranges such as the Himalayas.

Runny, low-silica magma makes gentle shield volcanoes; sticky, high-silica magma traps gas and makes explosive stratovolcanoes such as Mayon and Pinatubo. Hot spots, such as Hawaii, form volcanoes away from plate boundaries.

Example

Which magma makes explosive eruptions?

Sticky, gas-rich

Answer: high-silica magma

Example

What kind of boundary forms a mid-ocean ridge?

Plates move apart.

Answer: divergent

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all volcanoes erupt the same way.
  • Thinking hot spots are at plate boundaries.
  • Mixing up the lithosphere and the asthenosphere.

faq.q: Why does the Philippines have many volcanoes?
faq.a: Oceanic plates subduct beneath the islands, melt and form magma.

faq.q: How did the Cordillera mountains form?
faq.a: By plate collisions and volcanic activity that pushed and folded the crust upward over millions of years.

c: zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people

items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from landslides?

water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Which waves usually cause the most damage in an earthquake?
items.e: They have large amplitudes and travel along the surface.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 9 earthquake than a magnitude 6 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
What causes a tsunami?
c: a sudden movement of the sea floor, usually from a large undersea earthquake, which displaces water
items.e: Landslides and volcanoes can also cause them.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the risk of earthquake damage?
c: building codes that require flexible, reinforced structures
items.e: Planning and drills also help.

items.q: Why did the 1989 Newcastle earthquake cause so much damage despite a magnitude of only 5.6?
c: it was far from the city
it was shallow and close to a city, and some buildings were on soft sediments that amplified shaking
items.e: Thirteen people died.

items.q: What is liquefaction?
c: waterlogged sand or silt loses strength and behaves like a liquid during shaking
items.e: Buildings can sink or tilt.

items.q: What causes most earthquakes?
c: sudden movement along faults as stress built up between plates is released
items.e: The point of rupture is the focus.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from earthquakes?
c: monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 10 earthquake than a magnitude 7 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
What is the epicenter of an earthquake?
c: the deepest point of the fault
the place with the most damage always
the point on the surface directly above the focus
items.e: The focus (hypocenter) is underground.

Which kind of plate boundary forms volcanoes along the Andes?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?

a flat desert in the middle of a plate

items.q: Joy finds seafloor rock 800 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 8 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 800 km = 80,000,000 cm; ÷ 8 million years = 10 cm/yr.

items.q: How does an igneous rock form?
c: by magma or lava cooling and crystallizing
by heat and pressure changing another rock without melting
by layers of sediment being cemented
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: What drives the movement of tectonic plates?
c: the rotation of the core only
mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull
items.e: Slab pull at subduction zones is the strongest force.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

items.q: About how old is Earth?
items.e: 13.8 billion years is the age of the universe.

the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: divergent (plates move apart): new sea floor.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
items.e: S-waves cannot travel through it.

items.q: What is a mineral?

a substance made by living things

items.q: What is the principle of superposition?
c: in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the lowest layers are the oldest
all layers formed at the same time
the youngest layers are at the bottom
items.e: It gives relative ages.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms mid-ocean ridges?

items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: What do 4.4-billion-year-old zircons tell us about early Earth?
c: there was continental crust and probably liquid water very early
Earth had no crust for 2 billion years
items.e: Their oxygen isotopes suggest they formed with water present.

items.q: Evidence: GPS stations show Hawaii moving about 7 cm per year toward Japan. What does it support?
c: The rocks formed together before the continents split.
The continents may once have been joined.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Two plates slide past each other, as at the San Andreas Fault. What feature forms?
c: a trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands
a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
a deep trench and a chain of volcanic mountains
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

items.q: Evidence: Rock layers and mountain belts match across the Atlantic Ocean. What does it support?
c: New crust forms at the ridge and spreads both ways.
The southern continents were together near the South Pole.
The rocks formed together before the continents split.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: How does the greenhouse effect work?

items.q: Why does the land heat up faster than the sea?

items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Why do scientists keep revising the theory of plate tectonics?
c: New evidence from GPS, sea-floor mapping and earthquakes improves it.
items.e: Scientific theories develop with new evidence.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the layer of liquid iron and nickel?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
